summary: Proposes Limited Transmit, a TCP tweak that sends new data after the first duplicate acknowledgments. This helps recover from loss without waiting for a timeout, especially when the congestion window is small. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a friend says they missed one ball, you keep throwing a few more instead of waiting. This helps a lost piece get noticed sooner.

questions: faster loss recovery for small windows
what is fast retransmit in tcp
why does tcp need three duplicate acks
how does tcp recover from loss with a small window
subtitle: A small TCP tweak: send new data on the first two duplicate ACKs so a lost segment is found by Fast Retransmit instead of a slow timeout.

tldr.problem: When a TCP connection has a small congestion window, or many segments are lost in one window, too few duplicate ACKs arrive to trigger Fast Retransmit, so the sender must wait for a costly retransmission timeout.
tldr.mechanism: Limited Transmit has the sender send a new data segment on each of the first two duplicate ACKs, within a limit of 2 segments beyond the congestion window and without changing the window. This produces extra ACKs, so the standard threshold of three duplicate ACKs can be reached.
tldr.outcome: Loss is more often recovered by Fast Retransmit rather than by a timeout, and sending is less bursty. The RFC says the security impact is minimal.

facts.label: Extra data allowed
facts.value: Up to cwnd plus 2 segments outstanding

today: RFC 3042 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the congestion control rules of RFC 2581 and the base protocol in RFC 793.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3042 proposes the Limited Transmit algorithm, a small change to the sender side of TCP. It targets two situations: a connection whose congestion window is small, and one where a large number of segments are lost in a single transmission window.

The RFC notes that a small window can come from only a limited amount of data to send, from the receiver-advertised window, or from end-to-end congestion control on a connection with a small bandwidth-delay product. In these cases TCP's usual loss recovery does not work well.
sections.eli5: When only a few packets are in flight, TCP has a hard time noticing that one got lost. This RFC gives it a simple trick to notice sooner.

sections.title: Why Small Windows Recover Badly
sections.content:
TCP detects a missing segment in one of two ways. Either the acknowledgment (ACK) does not arrive in time and a retransmission timeout fires, or the Fast Retransmit algorithm resends a segment after three duplicate ACKs arrive. The sender waits for three because duplicate ACKs are also caused by packet reordering, and it wants to tell loss apart from reordering.

The minimum retransmission timeout is conservatively chosen to be 1 second, so a timeout is expensive. The RFC gives a concrete case: with a congestion window of three segments, one dropped segment produces at most two duplicate ACKs. Three are required to trigger Fast Retransmit, so the sender must wait for a timeout.
sections.eli5: A friend tells you a ball is missing only after three reminders. If you only threw three balls and one is lost, they can only remind you twice, so you wait a long time before trying again.

sections.title: The Limited Transmit Algorithm
sections.content:
When a TCP sender has previously unsent data queued, it SHOULD use Limited Transmit. The sender transmits new data when each of the first two consecutive duplicate ACKs arrives, provided two conditions hold:

  • The receiver's advertised window allows the segment to be sent.
  • The amount of outstanding data stays less than or equal to the congestion window plus 2 segments.

The congestion window (cwnd) MUST NOT be changed when these segments are sent. If the new segments and their ACKs are not dropped, they generate further duplicate ACKs, so the sender can still use the standard Fast Retransmit threshold of three. This is more robust to reordering than retransmitting an old segment on the first or second duplicate ACK.

With selective acknowledgments (SACK), the sender MUST NOT send new segments in response to duplicate ACKs that contain no new SACK information, because a misbehaving receiver could generate such ACKs.
sections.eli5: When your friend says they missed one, you throw up to two extra balls, but you never throw more than you are allowed. Those extra throws give your friend more chances to tell you which one was lost.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Burstiness
sections.content:
The RFC argues that Limited Transmit follows the conservation of packets principle. Each of the first two duplicate ACKs shows that a segment has left the network, and the sender has not yet decided that a segment was dropped, so it has no reason to think its congestion state is wrong.

Reordering is not rare. Because the earlier specification (RFC 2581) does not allow sending on the first two duplicate ACKs, a burst of segments goes out when an ACK for new data finally arrives after reordering. With Limited Transmit, segments are clocked out by incoming ACKs, so sending is less bursty.

The RFC cites a study of a busy web server in which roughly 56% of retransmissions were sent after the timeout expired, and 44% were handled by Fast Retransmit. Using this technique, 25% of the timeout-based retransmissions in that data would likely have been avoided.
sections.eli5: Each reminder from your friend means one ball has been caught, so you are allowed to throw one more. That keeps the game fair and stops you from throwing a big pile all at once later.

sections.title: Related Work: ECN and Rate-Halving
sections.content:
The RFC points to Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) as another way to help connections with small windows. ECN signals congestion without dropping segments, so the sender can avoid many Fast Retransmits and retransmission timeouts. When ECN-enabled traffic competes with non-ECN traffic, it can receive up to 30% higher goodput.

The Rate-Halving algorithm uses a form of limited transmit too. It sends a data segment on every second duplicate ACK, whereas Limited Transmit always sends a new segment on the second duplicate ACK that arrives.
sections.eli5: Other tricks exist too. One lets the network say "slow down" without throwing any ball away, and another sends an extra ball after every second reminder.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the additional security implications compared with TCP's existing weaknesses are minimal. The concern is "false" duplicate ACKs, which do not acknowledge new data. They can come from duplicated ACKs in the network or from a misbehaving receiver trying to subvert congestion control.

With SACK, the sender has fairly strong protection, because it can check that a duplicate ACK reports new data it actually sent. The most important protection is that the potential for harm is limited. A misbehaving receiver could send two duplicate ACKs after each regular ACK, but the sender may only exceed the congestion window by less than the duplicate ACK threshold of three segments. If at least a threshold number of duplicate ACKs arrive, a sender with Limited Transmit behaves essentially like one without it: the window is halved and loss recovery begins.
sections.eli5: A sneaky friend might shout fake reminders to make you throw more. But you are only allowed two extra throws, so the trick cannot make you flood the game.
